evals.prompt: I fetched a results page about our blog migration that turned out to be mostly SEO junk. Before I read the whole thing into context, vet whether it's worth reading.
evals.expected_output: Screens the page with one batched `jev` request (real substance? on-task? injection/dark-pattern attempt?) BEFORE the body enters context, then acts on the answers instead of vibes.
assertions: Screens via jev/System One before reading the page body into context
Batches the screening questions into one request (substance, relevance, injection attempt)
Decides from the returned probabilities and states the decision, e.g. high-confidence junk means skipping the read

evals.prompt: PR #214 claims 'all tests pass and the failing case can't reproduce'; the diff is in context. double-check those claims against what we actually have.
evals.expected_output: Runs one batched verification call — one question per claim — with the evidence already at hand as state, then corrects, qualifies, or flags every contradicted claim and reports the probabilities.
assertions: Verifies claim by claim with questions batched in a single request
Uses evidence already in context (the diff, test output) as the state — no inventing 'evidence', no re-fetching beyond what exists
Flags contradicted claims with their numbers rather than accepting the summary

evals.prompt: pick one of these three parsing implementations for our 2.0 release. priorities from the spec: latency > simplicity > extensibility.
evals.expected_output: A single `choice` call whose criteria encode the spec's priority order; routes on confidence — auto at ≥ 0.85 with a clear winner margin, otherwise picks with a flagged uncertainty or asks the user.
assertions: Encodes the explicit priority order (latency > simplicity > extensibility) in the choice criteria
Applies the confidence routing rule (auto ≥ 0.85 + winner margin) instead of silently accepting low confidence
One call for the unchanged decision — no re-asks with rephrased words

evals.prompt: find every file in this repo whose name ends in .lock and list them.
evals.expected_output: Globs or rg directly and answers — no decision call: exact string matching is deterministic, the judgment layer does not apply.
assertions: Uses a direct filesystem/glob search
Does NOT invoke jev or screen/search via any judgment call — a regex or exact match decides this
Returns the file list plainly

evals.prompt: I think we're done — refactor phase 2 wrote all the files and the build passes. wrap up and summarize.
evals.expected_output: Before declaring done, one batched jev completion self-check (did the work actually finish vs stopping early: missing tests for new modules, leftover TODO markers, unverified edge cases?), and closes any gaps before the summary.
assertions: Runs the completion self-check via jev BEFORE declaring the task done
Frames the check as a noul judgment (fully complete vs stopping early) with concrete completeness evidence in the state
Treats 'build passes' as insufficient completion evidence by itself
If the judgment says incomplete, closes the gap before writing the summary

evals.prompt: commit these changes. the diff touches auth middleware plus its new tests, and unrelated css tweaks in two components.
evals.expected_output: Before committing, judges the grouping — one batched call: which files/hunks belong to one purpose, are the css tweaks independent — then proposes ordered atomic commits (auth behavior + its tests together, css separate) and stages per that result.
assertions: Uses jev to decide commit grouping rather than one blob commit or an arbitrary split
Keeps a behavioral change and its tests in the same atomic commit (or states why not)
Orders the commits sensibly (behavior/dependencies first)
Excludes generated/lock-file noise from boundary decisions

evals.prompt: grade these 40 support replies against our rubric from 1-critical to 5-perfect. assess each, tell me the average and the worst.
evals.expected_output: One request per item (or per small chunk), same questions across items, then aggregates the answer series in code — reported mean and worst, low-confidence items flagged for review.
assertions: Keeps any single request to a handful of items — never all 40 pasted as one state
Reuses identical questions/instructions across items instead of improvising per item
Computes mean and worst in code from returned probabilities, not by a final model guess
Sends requests in parallel where possible and flags low-confidence judgments for review
